title: Can Small Language Models Plan Hospital Workflows Under Operational Constraints?
description:
Can a small language model generate practical hospital workflow plans when faced with real-world operational constraints?

This independent research project investigates whether small language models can produce feasible non-clinical hospital workflow plans when resources are limited or operational conditions are disrupted.

Using Qwen3-4B, I designed a pilot evaluation involving 15 fictional hospital scenarios covering power interruptions, software failures, limited computer availability, staff guidance, and incomplete records.

I compared the model's responses under two prompting conditions: standard prompting and constraint-aware prompting. The responses were assessed using a manually applied evaluation rubric covering constraint adherence, feasibility, assumption control, and adaptation specificity.

The experiment explores an important gap in AI evaluation: a response may sound reasonable while still proposing actions that are impractical under the conditions in which a person must actually work.

The project also proposes a path towards more reliable AI systems through targeted evaluation datasets, constraint-aware training examples, and explicit verification of generated plans.
Research Questions

Can a small language model recognise and respect operational constraints when planning non-clinical hospital workflows?

Does constraint-aware prompting improve the feasibility and reliability of its responses?

How could data curation, fine-tuning, and constraint verification improve performance?

Research Methodology

Selected Qwen3-4B as the open-weight model for evaluation.

Developed 15 fictional scenarios representing operational constraints in hospital environments.

Evaluated the model under standard and constraint-aware prompting conditions.

Collected and compared 30 model responses.

Applied a four-dimensional manual scoring rubric, with a maximum score of 8.

Analysed response quality and recorded constraint violations.

Developed recommendations for future dataset curation, model improvement, and verification.

Key Research Contributions

Problem Identification: Formulated an applied AI evaluation problem based on operational challenges in resource-constrained healthcare environments.

Evaluation Dataset: Designed a collection of 15 fictional scenarios for assessing operational reasoning.

Comparative Experiment: Evaluated model behaviour under two prompting conditions.

Manual Evaluation Framework: Developed a rubric covering constraint adherence, feasibility, assumption control, and adaptation specificity.

Improvement Proposal: Proposed constraint-focused data curation and explicit verification as directions for improving model reliability.
challenges:
Challenge 1: Translating a real-world problem into an evaluable research question

Hospital workflows involve multiple operational dependencies. A model might generate a plausible recommendation without considering whether the required resources are available.

Approach: Narrowed the investigation to non-clinical workflow planning and translated operational constraints into fictional, structured evaluation scenarios.

Challenge 2: Designing scenarios that test different types of constraints

A single scenario would not adequately test how the model responds to different operational disruptions.

Approach: Developed scenarios across five categories: power interruptions, software failures, computer availability, staff guidance, and incomplete records. Included a combined-constraint scenario.

Challenge 3: Evaluating responses beyond whether they sound convincing

Fluent language does not necessarily indicate that a proposed workflow is feasible.

Approach: Created a four-dimensional manual scoring rubric and separately tracked constraint violations to distinguish response quality from operational compliance.

Challenge 4: Interpreting results from a small pilot

A small evaluation cannot establish general model capability or support broad claims about all hospital environments.

Approach: Treated the experiment as an exploratory pilot, documented its limitations, and identified larger held-out evaluations as a necessary next step.
keyFeatures: Key Findings
This project is an exploratory evaluation, not a clinical validation study. Its results are limited to the selected model, scenarios, prompts, and manual scoring procedure.
The final published findings should include the verified comparison of both prompting conditions, the constraint-violation analysis, and the limitations of the experiment.
Proposed Future Work
Expand the evaluation dataset with more diverse and challenging operational scenarios.
Develop expert-reviewed reference plans and evaluation criteria.
Investigate supervised fine-tuning using constraint-aware examples.
Introduce an explicit constraint-verification stage after plan generation.
Evaluate improvements using held-out scenarios and additional models.

title: Battleground — AI-Powered Fighter Showdown
description:
Battleground is an interactive AI-powered web application that lets users compare two fighters, receive an AI-generated fight verdict, and view unique 16-bit pixel-art illustrations of each contender.

I built the application using Claude Code, applying an AI-assisted engineering workflow guided by Test-Driven Development (TDD) and structured implementation stages.

The application combines a lightweight Vanilla JavaScript frontend with Node.js serverless functions, integrating AI-powered decision-making, image generation, input validation, rate limiting, and browser-based data persistence.

A key part of the development process was using Claude Code as an engineering agent while maintaining control over architecture, implementation decisions, testing, and quality assurance.

The project demonstrates how AI coding agents can be used to build functional, full-stack web applications while applying established software engineering principles.
role: Full-Stack Developer, AI-assisted development using Claude Code.
challenges:
Challenge 1: Building a reliable AI-powered decision system

AI-generated responses can be unpredictable, malformed, or inconsistent. The application needed to guarantee that every valid fight produced a clear winner, including unusual comparisons such as identical fighters.

Solution: Implemented a structured AI judging system using Claude, with a Zod validation schema to enforce the expected response format. Winner identification is based on fighter position (A or B), rather than fighter name, allowing identical names to be handled correctly. A mock judging mode also allows the application to operate without an Anthropic API key.

Challenge 2: Protecting the AI system against prompt injection

Since users can enter arbitrary fighter names, malicious input could attempt to manipulate the AI judge's instructions.

Solution: Implemented input cleaning and validation, treating fighter names as data rather than instructions. Names are wrapped in dedicated tags, and the judge's system prompt explicitly instructs the model not to follow instructions embedded in fighter names.

Challenge 3: Managing external API failures without breaking the application

The application depends on external services for AI verdicts and image generation. A failure in image generation should not prevent users from receiving a fight result.

Solution: Designed the verdict and image-generation operations to run in parallel. Image failures are handled independently, with placeholder artwork displayed when an image cannot be generated. This allows the core fight experience to remain functional.

Challenge 4: Implementing reliable rate limiting in a serverless environment

Serverless functions can run on different instances, making in-memory rate limiting unreliable across requests.

Solution: Integrated Upstash Redis to enforce a limit of five fights per minute per visitor across serverless instances. Rate limiting is checked before making AI calls to prevent unnecessary API usage and reduce abuse.

Challenge 5: Efficiently storing fighter collections in the browser

Saving generated fighter images directly in browser storage could consume significant space.

Solution: Implemented the BattleDex collection using browser localStorage, compressing images into WebP format at approximately 5 KB per image before saving.
keyFeatures: AI-Powered Fight Verdicts: Compares two fighters and produces a winner with 2–4 sentences of playful reasoning using the Claude judging integration.
Mock Judging Mode: Keeps the application usable without an Anthropic API key through a built-in mock verdict system.
AI-Generated Fighter Artwork: Generates distinctive 16-bit pixel-art illustrations through the Pollinations API.
BattleDex Collection: Allows users to save and revisit favourite fighters using browser localStorage.
Image Compression: Compresses generated artwork into lightweight WebP images before storage.
Rate Limiting: Uses Upstash Redis to enforce five fights per minute per visitor.
Input Validation and Protection: Validates fighter names, handles identical fighters, and protects the AI judging prompt against prompt injection.
Parallel API Processing: Runs the fight verdict and fighter image-generation operations concurrently.
Responsive Design: Supports screens as narrow as 360px.
Accessibility: Respects reduced-motion preferences.
Graceful Error Handling: Provides dedicated feedback for rate limits, offline states, timeouts, invalid input, and failed verdicts.
